title: AI Agent Readiness Audit: Is Your Firm Ready for Workflow Automation?
subtitle: Score your firm in 12 minutes. Get a tier, a category breakdown, and a specific next move per workflow category.

answers.label: Operations Lead / COO / Head of Delivery

questions.text: Where does the data for your most painful workflow currently live?

answers.label: Single source of truth in one system
4+ systems, some in spreadsheets or email
Nobody can fully map where it lives

questions.text: When a new client, case, or project enters your pipeline, what percent of the intake data is structured (dropdowns, dates, numbers) vs. free text?
If you exported the last 90 days of intake data, how much manual cleanup would it need before an agent could process it?

low.headline: Your data is not agent-ready yet
low.text: Agents trained on messy, scattered inputs hallucinate, miss cases, and create more cleanup than they save. Fix the pipes before you hire the robot.
steps: Pick one workflow and map every data source it touches in a single diagram this week
Replace free-text intake fields with structured dropdowns and required fields in your primary system
Run a 90-day data audit to identify which fields are reliably populated vs. theatrical

mid.headline: Foundation is there, edges are rough
mid.text: You have the right systems but the seams leak. Agents will work on the happy path and fail on the 20% that needs cleanup. That ratio determines ROI.
steps: Document the 3 most common data quality failures and add validation at the source
Consolidate the 2-3 systems into a primary record with one-way sync from secondaries
Build a weekly 30-minute data hygiene ritual before automating anything downstream

high.headline: Your data layer is automation-grade
high.text: Clean inputs, structured fields, traceable sources. This is the substrate agents need. The bottleneck for you is not data, it is somewhere else in the audit.
steps: Pick your highest-volume workflow and pilot an agent on the last 90 days of data
Set up logging so every agent decision is queryable against the source record
Add anomaly detection on intake fields so data drift is caught before it poisons agents

questions.text: Can your best person explain, in a document, how they decide outcomes for this workflow?

answers.label: Yes, it's already documented and current
They could write it in a day
They'd struggle but could get 70% of it
Two senior people would give different answers

questions.text: What percent of cases in this workflow follow a predictable pattern vs. require creative judgment?
When a case goes wrong in this workflow, can you trace exactly which decision broke it?

answers.label: Yes, we have a post-mortem process
We argue about what went wrong

questions.text: How many of your top 3 decision-makers for this workflow would agree on the same edge case?

low.headline: The logic lives in heads, not systems
low.text: You cannot automate a decision that no two senior people make the same way. This is the most common reason agent pilots fail. Decisions must be written before they are coded.
steps: Sit your top 2 decision-makers down and walk through 10 recent cases on the whiteboard
Write a decision tree in plain language, not a flowchart, with the actual thresholds
Test the document by having a junior person apply it to 5 new cases and check the deltas

mid.headline: Documented but not battle-tested
mid.text: You have logic on paper but it has not been pressure-tested against edge cases. Agents will copy whatever ambiguity is in your doc, just faster and at scale.
steps: Run 20 historical cases through your documented logic and flag every disagreement
Add explicit branching for the top 3 edge cases that currently get handled by exception
Pilot the agent in shadow mode for 2 weeks before letting it act on its own

high.headline: Decision logic is ready to be encoded
high.text: Documented, consistent, traceable. This is the layer most firms get stuck on and you are past it. Your agent can encode actual judgment, not just rules.
steps: Convert your decision doc into prompt format with explicit thresholds and examples
Build a feedback loop where the agent flags low-confidence calls for human review
Set a quarterly review where the decision-makers update the logic based on new patterns

questions.text: How many times per week does the workflow you have in mind run across the team?
How much human time does one run of this workflow consume on average?
What is the business cost of a 24-hour delay on a single case in this workflow?

answers.label: Lost revenue or contract risk over $1,000

low.headline: Low-volume workflows are not worth automating yet
low.text: Agent builds carry a fixed cost in design, prompt engineering, and monitoring. Under a certain volume, automation is a hobby project, not a business decision.
steps: List your top 10 workflows by total weekly hours consumed across the team
Drop anything under 5 hours per week from the automation candidate list
Look at consolidating low-volume workflows into a shared template before automating

mid.headline: Volume is real but ROI is borderline
mid.text: You are in the zone where automation pays off in 6-9 months, not 6-9 weeks. The deciding factor is whether the workflow is growing or flat.
steps: Forecast whether this workflow doubles in the next 12 months based on pipeline
If growing, build now while the design effort is amortized over more future runs
If flat, consider a lightweight Zapier or n8n template before a full agent build

high.headline: High-volume, high-cost workflow worth automating
high.text: This is exactly the workflow profile where agents pay back in weeks not quarters. Your bottleneck is sequencing, not justification.
steps: Calculate the all-in monthly hours and multiply by a fully-loaded hourly cost in USD
Scope a 4-week pilot covering the 80% happy path, not the 20% edge cases
Set a success metric in hours-saved-per-week and review it weekly during the pilot

questions.text: Do the systems involved in this workflow have APIs or modern integrations you can use today?

answers.label: All systems have documented APIs we have used
Most have APIs, one is a screen-scrape job
Mostly legacy software with no API

questions.text: Does your IT or security function have clear policy on AI tools accessing your internal data?

answers.label: Yes, documented and we have an approved vendor
In progress, we have a working policy
No policy but the owner can make the call
Locked down, every tool needs a 3-month review

questions.text: How much automation infrastructure (Zapier, Make, n8n, custom scripts) is already running in your firm?

answers.label: A few Zapier zaps held together with hope

questions.text: Who would own the agent technically once it is live?

answers.label: A dedicated automation or ops engineer
An ops lead with technical comfort
The owner, in between client work
Nobody clearly, we would hope it just runs

low.headline: Your stack will fight you on this
low.text: Legacy systems, no APIs, and no clear owner means every agent build becomes a custom integration project. Costs balloon and reliability suffers. Fix the foundation first.
steps: Audit your current systems and tag each one as API-ready, scrapeable, or blocked
Add a Zapier or n8n instance and use it for 2-3 simple automations to build muscle
Identify or hire one person whose job includes owning automations end to end

mid.headline: Stack works, ownership is the gap
mid.text: You have the tools but not the operator. Agents that nobody owns end up unmonitored, drift in quality, and quietly create more work than they save.
steps: Name one person as the automation owner with at least 20% of their week protected
Set up a monthly review of all active automations with metrics on uptime and saved hours
Standardize on one platform (n8n or Make) rather than spreading across 3 tools

high.headline: Infrastructure ready for production agents
high.text: APIs, governance, mature automation stack, clear ownership. You can ship agents in 4-6 weeks instead of 4-6 months. The build is the easy part now.
steps: Add observability tooling so every agent run is logged, queryable, and alertable
Build a reusable agent template (prompt, tools, error handling) you can fork per workflow
Create a quarterly automation roadmap tied to business OKRs, not opportunistic builds

questions.text: How does your team feel about AI doing parts of their current job?

answers.label: Excited, they have asked for it

questions.text: If an agent gets a case wrong 1 out of 20 times in pilot, how does leadership react?

answers.label: That is expected, we will iterate
Concerned but supportive of the pilot

questions.text: Do you have a habit of running pilots, measuring, and iterating on internal tools?

answers.label: Yes, every quarter we ship and review
Rarely, we tend to set and forget

questions.text: Are you ready to redesign roles around what agents handle vs. what humans handle?

answers.label: Yes, role redesign is already on the roadmap
Open to it, no plan yet
We would prefer to keep current roles intact
Role changes are politically off the table

low.headline: Culture will sink the build before tech does
low.text: Agent deployments fail more from change resistance than from model errors. If the team is anxious and leadership is intolerant of pilot mistakes, you are not ready.
steps: Run a 60-minute session with the team to surface concerns about AI before any build
Pick a low-stakes workflow for the first pilot so failure costs are bounded
Have leadership publicly commit to a learning frame, not a perfection frame, on pilots

mid.headline: Open to change, light on muscle memory
mid.text: The team is curious but you have not built the iteration habit yet. The first pilot will be slower than expected. Treat it as capacity-building, not just an automation.
steps: Run the first pilot with a clear success metric and a 2-week iteration cycle
Share weekly pilot updates internally so the team sees how the agent improves
Plan a role conversation at week 6 about what humans now focus on instead

high.headline: Culture is your competitive advantage
high.text: Team is bought in, leadership tolerates pilot variance, you iterate as a habit. This is rarer than technical readiness and it is why your agent builds will compound.
steps: Set a goal of one new agent pilot per quarter with named owner and metric
Create a shared library of agent prompts and patterns the team can reuse and improve
Tie agent outcomes to comp or recognition so the iteration habit stays alive
